strengths: Significance: PMVB addresses a useful deployment problem: incorporating learned predictions into commercial MIP solvers through additional linear constraints. Its compatibility with different predictors and solvers is practically appealing.

Soundness: The four complementary subproblems preserve exactness when all branches are solved. Theorem 3.1 also provides a valid Chebyshev-based guarantee when its population mean and variance conditions hold.

Evaluation: Experiments cover logistic regression and GNN predictors, two commercial solvers, several combinatorial problems, and an IEEE-118 unit-commitment case. The reported 1.11–1.31× exact-solving speedups in Table 2 would be useful if established robustly.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript explains the main algorithm clearly and distinguishes its heuristic and exact-solving uses. Data sources, hardware, several solver settings, and a code repository are provided.

Limitations and ethics: The manuscript acknowledges the strong independence assumption and potential infeasibility of the data-free restrictions. No material research-ethics concern is evident from the described benchmark study.
weaknesses: Soundness—Theorem 2.1: The central concentration argument is not justified. Lemma 2.1 bounds prediction error averaged over new instances; it does not establish Equation (4) for a particular instance or conditional on membership in the prediction-dependent sets U and L. High marginal accuracy need not imply high accuracy among predicted positives. Moreover, independence conditional on a fixed instance, as stated in A4, does not establish the independence needed after averaging over instances. Consequently, the claimed optimal-solution containment guarantee does not follow from the stated assumptions.

Soundness—practical calibration: Theorem 3.1 requires population accuracy and variance conditions, but the manuscript does not provide a finite-sample procedure for certifying these after selecting the threshold. The experiments fix tau = 0.9 without explaining how Equation (9) is checked or reporting the variance bounds used. Remark 3.1 additionally strengthens the cuts by replacing threshold-based counts with sums of predicted probabilities; this strengthening does not inherit the theorem's guarantee without further calibration assumptions.

Soundness—data-free analysis: The proof of Theorem 4.1 bounds the number of LP-selected items omitted from the integer optimum, then claims the opposite-direction bound follows from complementarity. Knapsack solutions can have different cardinalities, so these two disagreement counts need not agree. The second inequality requires a separate argument. The concentration events used for both coefficient sequences also need explicit probability accounting.

Evaluation—selection of MIPLIB results: Section 5.4 reduces 132 instances to 57 by excluding infeasible restricted problems and cases where both runs time out. The reported 16% improvement therefore describes a selected subset and does not establish an overall benefit on the original benchmark. An evaluation of a complete procedure, including fallback behavior and its cost on excluded instances, is needed. Reporting the exclusions transparently is valuable, but it does not resolve this evidential limitation.

Evaluation—runtime and solution quality: Section 5.2 measures time to a target chosen retrospectively from PMVB's own 120-second run. This measures a particular time-to-target benefit, but without equal-budget objective gaps or primal-integral results it does not establish broader solution-quality improvements. Treatment of targets unreached by the baseline is unclear. No uncertainty estimates or repeated-seed results accompany the speedups, and SCUC uses only five test instances per setting.

Originality: The distinctive contribution is insufficiently isolated from existing local branching and prediction-centered neighborhood methods, including the cited Fischetti–Lodi and Ding et al. approaches. Comparisons primarily against unmodified solvers cannot determine whether the gains arise from the proposed probabilistic parameter selection or simply from restricting search around useful predictions. Comparisons using the same predictor with tuned local branching, variable fixing, and existing prediction-based search would substantiate the contribution.

Reproducibility and presentation: Important operational details remain unspecified, particularly variance estimation in the data-free setting, solver versions, random seeds, and whether prediction, root-LP computation, and subproblem setup enter reported runtimes. Large SCP training labels are permitted a 10% optimality gap, whereas the analysis assumes optimal-solution labels; this mismatch is not examined. Section 3.2 also reverses its pruning condition by saying the preferred region 'excludes' all optima, and Tables 3–4 use the unexplained name 'PreMIO'. These issues require clarification before the results can be reliably reproduced and interpreted.
